rows.title: Amazon dieback beyond the 21st century under high-emission scenarios by Earth System models
rows.study_objective: Using CMIP5 and CMIP6 ESMs that provide carbon cycle outputs extending beyond the 21st century, we investigate the timing, thresholds, mechanisms and implications of Amazon rainforest dieback under high-end RCP8.5 and SSP5-8.5 scenarios.
rows.existing_data_description: The data from the CMIP5 and CMIP6 simulations are available from the ESGF archive: https://aims2.llnl.gov/search/; Amazon geographical boundaries mask is available via EU SCIENCE HUB: https://forobs.jrc.ec.europa.eu/amazon; The MUltiscale Satellite remotE Sensing (MUSES) product for GPP was downloaded from the Zenodo archive https://zenodo.org/record/3996814; The ERA5 reanalysis data are available at https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu/datasets/reanalysis-era5-single-levels-monthly-means; the FLUXCOM-X-BASE GPP product.
rows.relationship_description: We performed a standardised (z-scored) logistic regression analysis showing that temperature is the dominant driver of dieback in most models, although precipitation exerts a strong influence in some; the timing of dieback onset shows a strong linear relationship with GSAT.
rows.threshold_description: On average, annual local surface air temperature above 32.2 +/- 4.8 degrees C and precipitation below 1394.3 +/- 306.0 mm year-1 are associated with the onset of the Amazon dieback.

rows.title: Amazonia as a carbon source linked to deforestation and climate change
rows.study_objective: Here we investigate Amazonia's carbon budget and the main drivers responsible for its change into a carbon source.
rows.existing_data_description: 2-m temperatures from ERA-Interim; GPCP precipitation versions 2.3 and 1.3; JPL monthly land mass grids of equivalent water thickness derived from GRACE; the MODIS Collection 6 MCD64A1 burned area product; PRODES products; 35 automatic meteorological field stations from INMET.
rows.relationship_description: We used maps of wi as spatial weighting functions for all studied parameters (temperature, precipitation, EVI, burned area, historical deforestation, and GRACE) to determine how each parameter influenced the carbon flux; the FCNBE value for ALF-SE indicates that it is a steadily increasing source, at a rate of 0.036 +/- 0.015 g C m-2 d-1 yr-1 (Pearson's correlation, r = 0.68, P = 0.045).
rows.dataset_description: 590 aircraft vertical profiling measurements of lower-tropospheric concentrations of carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide at four sites in Amazonia from 2010 to 2018; profiles extend from near the surface to approximately 4.5 km above sea level
rows.download_source: The CO2 VP data that support the findings of this study are available from PANGAEA Data Archiving, at https://doi.org/10.1594/PANGAEA.926834. Source data are provided with this paper.

rows.study_location: the Peruvian departments of Loreto, Ucayali and Madre de Dios, and the Brazilian cities of Porto Velho, Manaus and Santarem
rows.study_objective: Specifically, our objectives are to (1) explore how landings biomass, taxonomic and trait-based diversity (i.e. mean trophic level, body size, price and revenue) are changing across time in the Amazon and (2) use theoretical food web modelling to infer changes in fishery resilience and advance diagnostic tools for multi-species fisheries.

rows.relationship_description: Further theoretical analysis indicates that harvests can be maintained for a period of time but that continued biodiversity depletion reduces the pool of compensating species and consequently diminishes fisheries resilience.
rows.dataset_description: Landings taxonomic diversity and trait-based metrics for each region and year: we estimated evenness for each year, temporal beta diversity using the Jaccard dissimilarity index between the first year in each time series and each subsequent year, and landings biomass-weighted mean annual trait values for each region (mean trophic level, body size, price index and revenue index).

rows.existing_data_description: The VOD dataset is available from https://zenodo.org/record/2575599; the NDVI dataset is available from https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/metadata/geoportal/rest/metadata/item/gov.noaa.ncdc:C01558/html; the MODIS Land Cover dataset is available from https://lpdaac.usgs.gov/products/mcd12c1v006; the CHIRPS precipitation dataset is available from https://data.chc.ucsb.edu/products/CHIRPS-2.0/global_2-monthly/tifs; Brazilian road data are available from https://datacatalog.worldbank.org/dataset/brazil-road-network-federal-and-state-highways; SST data from HadISST are available from https://www.metoffice.gov.uk/hadobs/hadisst/.
rows.relationship_description: Resilience is being lost faster in regions with less rainfall and in parts of the rainforest that are closer to human activity.
rows.dataset_description: Changes in Amazon vegetation resilience since the 1990s and from 2003: lag-1 autocorrelation (AR(1)) computed in sliding windows from remotely sensed vegetation optical depth (1991-2016) at each grid cell, mapped as Kendall tau values of individual grid cells, together with the mean VOD AR(1) time series and the secondary variance indicator.
rows.download_source: All data and code used for the analysis are available on request from the corresponding author and are published online: Boulton, C. A. Amazon rainforest resilience data. Zenodo https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.5837469 (2022).

rows.study_objective: We estimate spatially explicit economic values for a range of ecosystem services provided by the Brazilian Amazon forest, including food production (Brazil nut), raw material provision (rubber and timber), greenhouse gas mitigation (CO2 emissions) and climate regulation (rent losses to soybean, beef and hydroelectricity production due to reduced rainfall).

rows.relationship_description: These changes in climate are used to estimate the impacts of deforestation on production and net returns of soybean production, beef production and hydroelectricity generation from four Brazilian facilities, using the Integrated Model of Land Surface Processes (INLAND).

rows.title: Sustainable land and irrigation management to limit loss of hydropower in the Andes-Amazon headwaters
rows.study_location: the upper Huallaga River in Peru
rows.study_objective: Here we develop a framework consisting of high-fidelity catchment and hydropower models while considering climate and other uncertainties in a robust, bottom-up manner for the upper Huallaga River in Peru. We then explore adaptation strategies across sectors.
rows.existing_data_description: Historic precipitation and air temperature data are obtained from Perus national gridded meteorological dataset, PISCO, for the years 1980-2020; 11 GCMs from the latest IPCC-CMIP generation (CMIP6) climate scenarios; daily discharge data from 2016-2020 at the Chaglla Dam site, from 2001 to 2015 at the Tingo Maria gauging station and from 2016-2020 at Higueras station.
rows.relationship_description: Our results highlight the strong dependence of hydropower outcomes on the management of upstream watersheds and notably on how upstream potato agriculture, the dominant crop in the region, is managed.
rows.dataset_description: Modelled hydropower outcomes for the Chaglla Dam from a dynamic daily timestep simulation of the water balance and reservoir allocations; the model generates information on both mean hydroelectric generation and firm power availability under 16 landuse/management scenarios and 18 climate scenarios.
rows.download_source: All data to reproduce the herein presented analyses are available at https://zenodo.org/record/8161594.
rows.code_source: The full code to reproduce analyses, run models, and produce figures is available on https://zenodo.org/record/8161594.

rows.title: Temperature boosts and constrains dung beetle diversity along an Andean-Amazonian elevation gradient
rows.study_location: the Kosñipata valley in southeast Peru
rows.study_objective: We tested the influence of temperature, moisture and food availability on the diversity of dung beetles (Scarabaeinae), food specialization and the mechanism of thermal limits along an Andean-Amazonian gradient from 250 to 3500 metres above sea level (m.a.s.l.).
rows.existing_data_description: Surface temperatures derived from the ECOSTRESS sensor; the NASA SRTMGL1 digital elevation model (v. 003); average body mass retrieved from Wilman et al.; the Barcode of Life Data Systems (BOLD) database for species identification; soil type and the composition of sand, silt and clay based on literature data, using the plots included in ABERG.
rows.relationship_description: Diversity showed no significant relationship with mammal biomass but increased with higher temperatures to 500 m.a.s.l., with a sharp drop at lower elevations.
rows.threshold_description: dung beetle abundance and species richness exhibited a hump-shaped pattern, with moderate richness in the lowlands, a peak at 500 m.a.s.l. and an exponential decline towards high elevations
rows.dataset_description: air temperature in the shade at 15 and 2 cm above the ground and soil temperature and moisture at -6 cm depth, recorded at 15 min intervals by one Temperature-Moisture-Sensor (TMS-4) on each plot, together with air temperature measured at 1.5 m height in 4 h intervals with iButton sensors, from which mean annual temperatures and soil moisture were calculated for each plot
rows.download_source: Data and code are publicly available in the FigShare repository (doi:10.6084/m9.figshare.30258298).
rows.code_source: Data and code are publicly available in the FigShare repository (doi:10.6084/m9.figshare.30258298).

rows.title: The drivers and impacts of Amazon forest degradation
rows.study_location: the pan-Amazon; the Amazon forest, excluding deforestation and savanna areas
rows.study_objective: In this Analytical Review, we: (i) identify proximate and underlying drivers of disturbances related to pan-Amazon forest degradation; (ii) provide estimates of uncertainties in the total degraded forest area; (iii) assess the ecological impacts of degradation; and (iv) discuss the distribution of benefits and burdens among stakeholder groups.
rows.existing_data_description: Published spatial datasets of the four main drivers of degradation - extreme drought occurrence, burned area, timber extraction and forest edge area (refs 23, 41-43, 130); previously published projections of edge effects (109), fire occurrence (112), timber extraction (42) and extreme drought (33); PRODES-INPE satellite monitoring of the Amazon forest.
rows.relationship_description: Disturbance type and intensity are strong predictors of the magnitude of change in above-ground carbon stocks, with single understory forest fires reducing aboveground carbon stocks by 13% to 50% and carbon losses in logged forests ranging from 4% to 35%.
rows.dataset_description: First-order spatially explicit 2019-2050 projections of potential future patterns of degradation of the Amazon forest and their effects on carbon stocks, produced by combining previously published projections of the individual main disturbances, under the governance (GOV) and business-as-usual (BAU) deforestation scenarios.

rows.title: Weather disasters and their underreported transboundary impacts on Amazonian communities
rows.study_location: Amazonia municipalities across five Amazonian countries (Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador, Bolivia and Peru)
rows.study_objective: To quantify regional impacts, we compiled and analyzed reports on weather disaster category, frequency, human, and economic impacts from 2013 to 2023 across five Amazonian countries.
rows.existing_data_description: Municipal-scale counts of reported disasters were modeled as functions of precipitation (CHIRPS [12]), elevation (SRTM 90m Digital Elevation Data [13]), human population [14], and hot pixels [15].
rows.relationship_description: Spatial negative binomial regressions linked reported disaster counts to remotely sensed variables: all modeled disaster categories were positively associated with human population density, days per year with rainfall >=20 mm were positively associated with floods and landslides, mean elevation with landslides, and hot pixels with wildfires.
rows.dataset_description: Municipality-level weather disaster reports for 2013-2023 retrieved from government sources in Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador, Bolivia and Peru, standardized between countries and categorized into storms, floods, landslides, droughts and wildfires, with the economic, infrastructure and human losses retrieved from the reports linked to each disaster.
